_embed_throughput_comment: Indexing is GPU-bound; these keys feed the embedder (CLI --embed-batch/--embed-inflight > config > defaults 128/2). Defaults suit a heavy model (a 4B saturates the GPU on one batch). A small/fast embedder (e.g. jina-code-0.5b) starves on them -- raise both (512/8 works well) and raise llama-server --parallel to match, keeping --ctx-size/--parallel >= your largest chunk. Tune against the run summary's chunks/s. See DOCS.md 'Indexing throughput'.
_exclude_comment: No excludes ship as hardcoded defaults in the code -- they're inherently per-codebase (a vendored SDK under a junk-looking path like .nuget/ may be legit content). This list is the recommended starting point for a fresh setup; curate it per codebase. Common candidates to add: .venv/, venv/, node_modules/, __pycache__/, .git/, .claude/, dist/, .next/, target/, and any other dependency-install or build-output directory in your repo.
_include_comment: Re-admits a subtree under an excluded prefix -- e.g. "thirdparty/embree/" re-admits that vendored library even though thirdparty/ is excluded above. Empty by default.
_edge_type_weights_comment: Top-level (not nested under repomap/research) -- shared by repomap.py's index-time PageRank and research.py's structural boost/graph-expansion. All 1.0 (shown here) is the default and reproduces the previous behaviour exactly -- edge_type is one of calls/imports/inherits/xlang (extracted facts), associated (inferred, but PMI-selected as the high-signal top slice of mentions -- see associated_top_frac below), or mentions (inferred name co-occurrence, most edges on a large corpus, the noisiest signal). Weights only take effect for PageRank after the next index run (chunker.py persists PageRank at index time); research reads this map live on every /research call. POST /research also accepts a per-request edge_type_weights field that overrides this config-level map for that call only (request > project config > all-1.0 default); the MCP codebase_research tool's 'scope' parameter drives this. See DOCS.md.
_embed_watchdog_secs_comment: Top-level, default 300. If no embedding batch commits within this many seconds, index_paths aborts the run loudly with a NoProgressError naming the last-progress timestamp and embedder URL, instead of hanging forever on a wedged embedder. Resets on every batch commit (success or failure), so a legitimately slow batch never trips it -- raise it if your embedder's genuine per-batch latency is high.
_cap_mentions_fanout_comment: Top-level, default false. When true, the mentions pass of build_refs skips any referenced name with more than 8 definer chunks (same skip-the-whole-name rule the xlang/typed passes already apply) instead of fanning out to every definer. On a large corpus, a few hundred ubiquitous names such as Update or Init can account for most of the graph's edges. Trade-off: find_usages loses mention edges for those names (typed edges already skip them; find_symbol still resolves them precisely). Enabling on an existing index requires `chonks index --rebuild-graphs` (graphs only, no re-embed).
_associated_top_frac_comment: Top-level, default 0.02 ('PMI-pruned mentions'). The mentions pass' (chunk, referenced name) population is PMI-ranked -- a focused chunk naming a rare name scores high, a wall-of-names chunk naming a ubiquitous name scores low -- and its top associated_top_frac fraction is labelled 'associated' instead of 'mentions'; the label change is the ONLY effect (edge_type_weights' associated default is 1.0, same as mentions, so ranking is untouched until you deliberately weight them apart). 0 disables entirely -- bit-identical chunk_refs to pre-PMI behaviour. Only the full-rebuild path (chonks index --rebuild-graphs, or a run that falls through build_refs' incremental-update gate) applies PMI labeling; the incremental path never promotes, so an existing index's associated labels reflect the last full graph build until the next --rebuild-graphs -- see repomap.build_refs' docstring.
_file_cap_comment: search.file_cap (semantic mode only): caps chunks per path in the returned top_k, backfilling freed slots from the next-ranked chunks of other files -- stops a near-duplicate wall of one hot file (e.g. a heavily-referenced symbol's own chunk repeated by near-identical surrounding context) from consuming most of the result set. 0 (shown here) is the default and reproduces the uncapped behaviour exactly. POST /search also accepts a per-request file_cap field that overrides this config-level value for that call only (request > project config > 0/off default).
